ANIMAL CATEGORIES LESSON · ANIMAL CATEGORIES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Reptiles — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the scaly family and its sunshine secret, one reptile at a time.

What is this?

Reptiles are the scaly animals — snakes, crocodiles, chameleons, lizards and their kin — with dry, scaled skin and bodies that warm up in the sun.

What does it mean?

Cold-blooded is the key idea, said kindly: reptiles run on sunshine the way we run on food — the morning basking session IS their breakfast.

What does the child need to know?

Snakes have no legs at all and "hear" through their jawbones; crocodiles have the strongest bite ever measured in a living animal; chameleons change color to talk and to hide; lizards do push-ups — a real signal that means "this rock is mine".

Why this matters

Reptiles are the closest living look at the dinosaur age — same scales, same rules — and children adore the connection.

What it teaches

Understanding body-temperature differences across animals, signal-reading (push-ups and color changes are messages), and safe-distance respect for wild reptiles.

Words to learn

reptilescalescold-bloodedbasksnakecrocodilechameleonlizardcamouflagejaw

Say this to your child

“"Reptiles wear scales and run on sunshine! The snake slithers with no legs at all, the crocodile has the strongest bite, the chameleon changes color to talk, and the lizard does push-ups on its rock. Morning sun, then breakfast!"”

Step by step

  1. The scale rule: reptiles wear dry scales — no fur, no feathers. Touch a toy snake: that texture is the family trademark.
  2. The sunshine rule: reptiles wake up cold and bask to warm their engines — a morning sunbathe is their breakfast.
  3. The snake: zero legs, and it moves anyway — s-shaped ripples. It "hears" vibrations through its jaw on the ground.
  4. The crocodile: the jaw — bite force champion, and it lurks like a floating log with eyes. Respect from a distance, always.
  5. The chameleon and the lizard: the chameleon changes color to send messages and to vanish; the lizard does push-ups — a real signal that means "this rock is mine".

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the snake curves through its whole square, the crocodile shows its toothy grin, the chameleon grips a branch with its mitten feet and curled tail, and the lizard does its push-up on a warm rock.

Ask your child

"How does a reptile warm up?" (basking in the sun) "Which reptile has no legs?" (the snake) "What does the chameleon change?" (its color — to talk and to hide)

What your child can say or do

Your child might do lizard push-ups on any warm patio stone, slither across the carpet with perfect S-arms, or explain to a grandparent that cold-blooded means "sun-powered, not grumpy".

Out in the real world

Zoo reptile houses have basking lamps that show the sunshine rule live — look for the lizard parked under the light at opening time. In warm US states, lizards do push-ups on garden walls all summer.

Try it together

Reptile charades: slither, chomp slow-motion, color-change walk (cushion to cushion, changing your "color" word at each), and the push-up finish. The audience guesses; the rock stays warm.

Understanding check

Ask: "What covers a reptile’s skin?" (dry scales) "Why do they bask?" (to warm their bodies) "What does the lizard’s push-up mean?" ("this rock is mine!")

This lesson pairs with the Reptiles flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animal Categories.
